newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia metals/oil exports won't see low costs soon.
newsitem.headline: Russia metals/oil exports won't see low costs soon.

text.p: Russian electricity, rail transport and gas costs are unlikely to cheer domestic metals and oil exporters by coming down soon, despite President Boris Yeltsin's attack on high prices, analysts said Thursday.

Some of the biggest winners from monopolies' tariff cuts would be giant, power-guzzling aluminium smelters -- the biggest of which, Bratsk and Krasnoyarsk, are in southern Siberia, thousands of rail miles from western markets.
"Obviously tariff cuts would be good for Russian industry, especially for large consumers of electricity, like metal plants," said Anton Kudryashov, head of equity trading at Renaissance Capital.
"But it will take time, by which I mean one to two years."

Yeltsin, in a state-of-the-nation address to parliament and key economic policy statement, singled out the natural gas, electricity and rail transport monopolies for charging too much, fuelling a non-payments crisis and stifling enterprises.
His comments were vague, but any cuts would be significant for the world's largest aluminium exporter and third-largest oil exporter.
Electricity is a major cost in aluminium production in Russia, which already has some of the world's highest tariffs, and lower rates could free up cash to boost output.
Rail transport tariffs covering this vast country's 11 time zones are key for exporters and higher rates have cut into resources needed to reverse steep oil output declines.
But analysts doubted the changes Yeltsin called for were imminent.

"I think the actual implementation of any changes to electricity prices will take quite a while and would be different for different regions," said Alexander Kazbegi, Russian utilities analyst at Salomon Brothers on London.
But he said the government's long-term plan was to make industrial electricity users pay less in real terms and residential customers more.
Some analysts said Yeltsin's comments slamming monopolies could have implications for Russian oil exports.

"What is interesting is that we are likely to see more power going to the Federal Energy Commission," said Stephen O'Sullivan, oil and gas director at MC Securities, referring to the state regulatory body that is trying to inject market principles into energy monopolies.
"This could affect oil as well, because the commission ought to look at Transneft tariffs, Gazprom tariffs, as well as rules governing access to (oil and gas) pipelines," he said.
State-owned Transneft controls the national oil pipeline system and has the power, partly through tariffs, to affect oil producers and exporters' bottom lines.
"Western and Russian companies have complained about the high Transneft tariffs," O'Sullivan said. "You could also see more transparency in access to oil pipeline space."

Russia's natural gas monopoly RAO Gazprom and national power grid operator Unified Energy System (UES) both said that any sharp reduction in the rates they charge would mean a cut in supplies on the Russian market.
Gazprom 0#GAZP.RTS spokesman Anatoly Kotov told Reuters that if forced to charge lower prices, Gazprom's output -- and presumably, its giant exports to Europe -- would slip.
"A sharp fall in prices will lead to difficulties in gas deliveries," he said.

UES 0#EESR.RTS spokesman Alexander Tarankov said lower prices would mean less money to buy heavy fuel oil and natural gas to fuel power stations and less electricity for regions without their own generators.
He said a cut in electricity prices without a corresponding drop in prices for heavy fuel oil could make the supply blackouts common in Russia's Far East a nationwide phenomenon.
